correctness.rationale: Each nonempty proper cycle subset has boundary size twice its number of cyclic components, and singleton cuts already have size 2. Thus feasible prefixes are cyclic intervals, with a root and n−2 independent end choices, then a forced last vertex. Only the intermediate prefix of a swap changes. At the first swap the root moves one step and the first bit flips, at the last the final bit flips, and internally precisely adjacent unequal bits may be exchanged. This also holds at n=3, when the two boundary swaps are distinct and there are no internal swaps. Degree is two plus the number of switches, so the binomial distribution and edge count follow. Particles can be moved right and removed, connecting each root layer, and first swaps connect the roots. For fixed equal roots, bringing the next target vertex left preserves connectivity: it is adjacent to the agreed prefix, contained in every changed prefix with that vertex inserted. Each such swap removes one Kendall inversion; every adjacent-swap path costs at least the Kendall distance. Between all-one states, equal interior occupancies force equal signed net flux F through every one of the n−1 interfaces, with F≡k modulo n because of the root change. This gives the lower bound (n−1)min(k,n−k); passing a vacancy across the word advances the root by one in n−1 swaps, and reversal of that path retreats by one. The unconstrained distance counts the k(n−k) inverted pairs between the two rotated blocks, yielding the claimed excess. Fresh permutation enumeration used explicit cycle-edge boundary sizes and BFS and confirmed the counts, connectivity, rotations and all root-zero pairs for 3≤n≤8 (root symmetry handles the other labels). This is finite corroboration, not an all-pairs or all-size numerical proof.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: For clockwise rotations, choose v as the order with starting label advanced by k and u the other. Their difference is z=(k,0,…,0,n−k) for 0<k<n. Every proper prefix containing the first bucket has sum k, so no inner pivot exists. The two weighted sums are (m+1)(n−k) and (m+1)k, giving precisely the claimed distance with m=n−2; k=0 is trivial. The Kendall count and quadratic excess are then arithmetic. The fixed-root insertion uses only the known interval-order characterization and the standard inversion argument. Neither this nor counting switches yields a distinct nonmechanical remainder.
